title: Secret Righteousness, the Lord's Prayer, and Freedom from Worry
summary: Jesus warns against practicing righteousness to be seen, applying the warning to giving, prayer, and fasting, and at the center he teaches his disciples the Lord's Prayer. He then calls them to store up treasure in heaven rather than on earth, to keep their eye sound, and to see that no one can serve both God and money. The chapter closes with the command not to worry about food and clothing, since the Father who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies knows what his children need, and to seek first his kingdom and righteousness.
story: The Sermon on the Mount continues. Chapter 5 described a righteousness greater than that of the scribes and Pharisees, reaching to the heart in how disciples treat others. Chapter 6 turns to how that righteousness relates to God: acts of devotion done for the Father rather than for an audience, and a life whose treasure, loyalty, and trust are fixed on him. The phrase your Father, or your Father in heaven, runs through the chapter more than in any other part of Matthew, and it is the key to the whole: disciples live before a Father who sees in secret, knows their needs, and rules a kingdom they can seek above everything else. Chapter 7 will close the sermon with warnings about judgment and the call to act on Jesus' words.
historical:
Giving to the poor, prayer, and fasting were the three great practices of Jewish piety in the Second Temple period. The book of Tobit, a Jewish writing from the last centuries before Christ, joins prayer, fasting, and almsgiving as marks of righteousness, and later rabbinic writings treat charity as among the highest duties. Pious Jews prayed at set times each day, often reciting the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4-9) and a series of blessings, and some Pharisees fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12). Jesus does not criticize these practices; he assumes his disciples will do them (when you give, when you pray, when you fast) and addresses their motive.

The Lord's Prayer resembles Jewish prayers of the time in several phrases. The Kaddish, an ancient Aramaic prayer still used in synagogues, asks that God's great name be magnified and sanctified and that he establish his kingdom within the lifetime of those who pray, though its exact wording in the first century is uncertain. Luke records a shorter form of the Lord's Prayer given in response to a disciple's request (Luke 11:2-4). The familiar closing doxology, for yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever, is not found in the earliest manuscripts of Matthew; a form of it appears in the Didache, an early Christian manual, and it entered later manuscripts from the church's liturgical use.
cultural:
The word hypocrite originally meant a stage actor, one who played a part behind a mask, and Jesus applies it to religion performed for spectators. The trumpet of verse 2 may be a vivid figure of speech for self-advertisement; some scholars connect it with the trumpet-shaped offering chests in the temple courts, though that link is uncertain. Most homes had one inner storeroom without windows, the inner room of verse 6, the most private space in a house. Fasting was often accompanied by signs of mourning, such as not washing and putting ashes on the head, so someone fasting could be recognized; Jesus tells his disciples to wash and anoint their heads as for an ordinary day.

Wealth in that world was stored in cloth and garments, which moths could ruin, or in metals and goods that could corrode, and thieves could break in by digging through the walls of a house. The idea of a good or bad eye (verses 22 and 23) is a Jewish idiom: an evil eye meant stinginess or envy, and a good or single eye meant generosity and undivided focus. Money in verse 24 translates mammon, an Aramaic word for wealth or property, here personified as a rival master. Lilies of the field were the wildflowers of Galilee, and dried grass was used as fuel for clay ovens.
literary: The first half of the chapter (verses 1 to 18) is carefully structured. Verse 1 states the principle, and then three matching paragraphs apply it to giving, prayer, and fasting, each with the same pattern: do not act like the hypocrites, they already have their full reward, but you do it in secret, and your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you. Into the middle paragraph Jesus inserts the Lord's Prayer and a comment on forgiveness, so that the prayer sits at the center of the whole Sermon on the Mount. The prayer itself has an address and six petitions, the first three concerned with God's name, kingdom, and will, and the last three with our bread, our debts, and our testing. The second half (verses 19 to 34) is a series of short sayings joined by the theme of undivided loyalty, arguing from the lesser to the greater (if God clothes the grass, how much more you) and ending with the central command to seek first the kingdom.

outline.t: Do not practice righteousness to be seen
Treasure, the eye, and two masters
Do not worry: seek first the kingdom

doctrines.note: Prayer is addressed to a Father who already knows what his children need. Its first concern is God's name, kingdom, and will, and only then our bread, forgiveness, and protection.
The Father feeds the birds and clothes the lilies, and his care for his children is greater still. Trust in his provision frees disciples from anxious striving without making them idle.
Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness. The kingdom is to be prayed for (Your kingdom come) and sought above every other good, and it reorders every other desire.
No one can serve two masters. Wealth is presented as a rival god that demands loyalty, and Jesus calls his disciples to undivided allegiance.

words.note: Epiousios, translated daily. The word is almost unknown outside the Lord's Prayer; Origen, in the third century, thought the Gospel writers had coined it. Suggested meanings include for today, for the coming day, and necessary for existence. Jerome's Latin translation rendered it supersubstantial in Matthew and daily in Luke. The simple request for the day's bread fits the context of trust.

Opheilema, debt. Luke's version says sins (Luke 11:4). In Aramaic, the language Jesus likely spoke, the same word could mean both a debt and a sin, and Jewish teaching often pictured sin as a debt owed to God. The petition asks God to cancel what we cannot repay.

Merimnao, to be anxious or worry. It appears six times in verses 25 to 34. It describes a mind divided and pulled apart by fear about the future, which is why it belongs with the warnings about serving two masters.

Mammonas, wealth, from an Aramaic word for money or possessions. Jesus personifies it as a master who competes with God for service. The warning is not that money is evil in itself but that it demands the loyalty that belongs to God alone.

christ: Jesus teaches his disciples to call God Our Father in heaven, sharing with them the relationship he himself has with the Father. The Gospels show Jesus praying this way himself: in Gethsemane he addresses God as My Father and prays that the Father's will be done (26:42), the very petition he taught. The petition Your kingdom come is answered in Jesus' own ministry and will be completed at his return. The forgiveness his disciples ask for is secured by his death, which he describes as his blood poured out for the forgiveness of sins (26:28). His life also embodies the chapter's teaching: he had no place to lay his head (8:20), sought first his Father's kingdom, and entrusted himself to the Father's care even to death.

hard.q: Does verse 15 mean God's forgiveness depends on our forgiving others?
hard.a: Jesus says plainly that if we do not forgive others, our Father will not forgive us, and the parable of the unforgiving servant makes the same point (18:21-35). This can sound as if forgiveness is earned. Most interpreters answer that the relationship runs the other way: God's forgiveness comes first as a gift, as the parable shows when the king cancels a vast debt before the servant does anything, but a person who has truly received mercy will show it. A heart that refuses to forgive reveals that it has not grasped or accepted the forgiveness it claims. Some traditions emphasize the warning more strongly, others the priority of grace, but across Christian traditions the teaching is taken seriously: forgiving others is not optional for those who pray the Lord's Prayer. Forgiveness in this sense does not require pretending that harm did not happen or restoring trust to someone who remains dangerous; it means releasing the debt and the claim to revenge.

questions: Which of your religious practices would change if no one else could ever see them?
Pray the Lord's Prayer slowly, one petition at a time. Which request is hardest for you to mean, and why?
Jesus says your heart follows your treasure. Looking at where your money and worry go, what does it suggest your heart is attached to?
